items.originalTitle: Oklahoma GOP governor warns of growing socialist tendencies on the right
items.author: Lauren Fedor
items.title: Oklahoma GOP governor warns of growing socialist tendencies on the right
items.summary: Oklahoma’s Republican governor warned against populist economic ideas gaining popularity, as he called for fellow Republicans to reject socialism and embrace free markets and an “ownership economy.” “A socialist or a populist economy is something that is not American,” Gov. Kevin Stitt said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. “We should all be concerned about the amount of people that think that socialism is the answer.” When asked if he was concerned about socialist tendencies on the right, Stitt criticized fellow Republicans who have called for data center moratoriums.. “When you start dictating … you see some people from the far right saying, ‘Well, we don’t want data centers. We don’t want that,’” Stitt said. “When did we become a party that if you follow all the rules, you follow the permitting, the clean water, the clean air, and you own your own land, that we allow the government to tell you what you can do on that property?” the Oklahoma governor asked. “That is what I'm talking about, that we need to be very, very careful about.” Stitt also called on President Donald Trump to use his final two years in the White House to push for bipartisan immigration reform — his latest remarks on the topic. “We need to have a strong border. We need to know who is coming into our country. We need to vet those people,” Stitt told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson. “He can lead on this, he can fix this immigration policy. “To me, we are overthinking it,” Stitt added. “It is as simple as: If an employer is vouching for an employee, the state governors should be able to issue that workforce permit. Period, end of story.” Stitt described Trump as a “business person” who “understands the need for a workforce.” But he blamed Congress and other interests in Washington for standing in the way of reform. “It's not that complicated. But the problem is Washington, D.C., each side thinks they're winning on it. They raise money off of it. They politic off of it. They try to crush the other side over these issues instead of fixing it for the American people,” Stitt said. “That's why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.”

items.originalTitle: Utah GOP governor on Trump and 2028: ‘It’s time for the next thing’
items.author: Lauren Fedor
items.title: Utah GOP governor on Trump and 2028: ‘It’s time for the next thing’
items.summary: Utah’s Republican governor wants his party to move beyond President Donald Trump heading into the next presidential election. “It’s time for the next thing,” Gov. Spencer Cox said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. Cox called on his fellow Republicans to start looking for new leadership in the wake of this month’s midterm election defeats. “This is how this works when presidents move on. We should be looking for the next leadership in our party and what that looks like,” Cox told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson. “We’ve got JD Vance and Marco Rubio, and those seem to be kind of the two choices now,” Cox said, referring to the Vice President and Secretary of State, respectively. “But I think you’ll see a lot of people step up … there are a lot of really interesting folks.” “I’m a fan of governors,” Cox added. “I think governors with executive experience are the best to lead the country.” Vance told Fox News earlier this week that he would decide “sometime next year” whether he will run for president in 2028. Rubio has dismissed suggestions that he would launch his own bid, and has said he would support Vance if the Vice President ran for the White House. “I am hopeful that there are some Republican governors that will throw their hat in,” said Cox, a two-term governor. “We can have a competition of ideas heading in to find out what's next.” Cox said that Trump still has a “really important role to play” in leading the party over the next two years, adding that the president still had an “opportunity” to strike bipartisan deals on permitting reform and other policy areas in his last two years in office. Cox called the president “unique,” adding: “He’s someone who has the attention of the country in a way that almost no president has had in my lifetime.” “People really love him or really don’t like him, but everybody’s paying attention to him,” he said.

items.originalTitle: This new early-state governor has advice for 2028 Democratic hopefuls
items.author: Alec Hernandez
items.title: This new early-state governor has advice for 2028 Democratic hopefuls
items.summary: Deb Haaland is about to take the helm of a newly-minted Democratic presidential primary battleground. She has thoughts for her party’s White House hopefuls on how to win there. Haaland, New Mexico’s incoming governor, told POLITICO that immigration will be a “top issue” in the presidential election — one that she’s “anxious” to see how future candidates plan to address — and said that engaging with rural voters in her state will be key to any successful primary campaign. “New Mexico is the fifth largest state, and we are largely rural,” Haaland told POLITICO’s Erin Doherty in an onstage interview at the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah. “There are far more rural communities than there are large cities in our state, and so this will be important for New Mexicans to to really understand or to really know that any presidential candidate understands the challenges that they're facing.” Immigration is “going to be a top issue with the 2028 presidential election,” she added. “New Mexico is an early primary state, and it happens that we're a border state, too.” Haaland’s ascension to the governor’s mansion coincides with a major change in New Mexico’s place in the Democratic Party's presidential nominating calendar pecking order. The state will now be fourth in the voting calendar behind South Carolina, Nevada and New Hampshire. The move gives New Mexicans — and their new governor — significant influence in shaping the kind of nominee the party selects to take back the White House. It’ll also pose a significant test for candidate’s engagement with Latino voters, as New Mexico ranks first nationwide in its population share of Latino residents. Some of those potential candidates have already come calling. “Rahm Emanuel was in New Mexico, and he did quite a bit of traveling around,” Haaland said, noting that several senators made their own sojourns to the state for an event hosted in October by Democratic Sen. Ben Ray Luján in Alberquerque. Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg made his own trip to the state in September. “Whether all of them are running for president, I can't tell you, but I am really anxious to see who does.” Haaland, a former Secretary of the Interior and the first Native American woman elected to a governorship, is ready to wield her own influence in the process as well, flexing her new power broker status . “I would love to endorse, but I'll wait and see who throws their hat in the ring,” she said. Haaland was swept into office with a historic number of fellow Democrats across the country on a mandate to deliver on affordability. It’s the “biggest issue” in New Mexico, Haaland said, adding that her priority to deliver lower costs for New Mexicans will start with expanding access to affordable health care. “Right now we're talking with some of the leaders in the legislature about health care, a public option for people in New Mexico,” she said. “Health care is a top top priority.”

items.originalTitle: Bo French loses Texas country club membership
items.author: Casey He and Jonathan Martin
items.title: Bo French loses Texas country club membership
items.summary: Bo French, the far-right firebrand who centered his losing campaign for the Texas Railroad Commission on his anti-immigration stance, lost his membership at a Fort Worth country club, according to a letter obtained by POLITICO . The letter from River Crest Country Club, dated Nov. 10 and addressed to French, said the club’s board of directors voted to terminate French’s membership immediately “for reasons relating to the reputation and general welfare of the Club.” French said Wednesday on social media that the board asked him to resign in September due to "racist posts." He said he refused to do so, leading to an expulsion meeting. "Nothing I said in September was racist," he said in a published statement that he read to the board. The country club, founded in 1911, is the eighth to open in the state and boasts being a “who’s who” of Fort Worth. It hosts a 6,368-yard golf course that has been a training ground for top golfers, according to its website. River Crest declined to comment, citing its policy of not doing so about “past, present and prospective members” and club operations, its general manager said in an email. French, who has a history of making controversial statements on immigration issues like the H-1B visa program, made headlines in September after going viral on social media for a post he made that appeared to disparage Asian American students at the University of Texas at Austin. His remarks capitalized on the growing anti-Indian sentiment sweeping Texas and across the nation , particularly against holders of the high-skilled worker visa, a majority of whom are from India. The post quickly drew rebukes from Democrats and some Texas Republicans, who denounced it as racist. But French stood by the post . He said he was criticizing admission and hiring policies at UT, the state’s public flagship, that he claimed discriminated against Texas residents. (State law requires a majority of admitted students at the school to be residents of the state.) French lost by 677,000 votes in his bid to sit on the influential statewide body that regulates Texas’ oil and gas industry two months later amid a statewide wipeout for the GOP. He previously led the Tarrant County Republican Party and also had two unsuccessful state House bids. French did not respond to requests for comment sent to multiple email addresses associated with him. Ashley Ahn contributed reporting.
